# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory era), ca. 1798–1819

## Jurisdiction Overview
The area now called Alabama was administered as the **Mississippi Territory** from 1798 to 1817 (created from land ceded by Georgia and from former Spanish West Florida), then as the **Alabama Territory** from 1817 until statehood in 1819. Before 1798, the Mobile coastal strip passed through French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), and Spanish (1780–1813) control, while the interior was Creek/Muscogee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw territory.

> ⚠️ **Key jurisdictional warning:** Records from this period will not be filed under "Alabama." Search under **Mississippi Territory** for anything before 1817, and be ready to work in Spanish or French for colonial-era Mobile material.

---

## Boundary Changes
- The Mississippi Territory originally covered only a narrow strip along the 31st–32nd parallels, then expanded in 1804 and again in 1812 to include all of present-day Alabama and Mississippi.
- In 1817 it split: the western half became the state of Mississippi; the eastern half became the Alabama Territory (→ state of Alabama in 1819).
- For an event in present-day Alabama, search **Mississippi Territory** (pre-1817), **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819), or the state of Alabama (post-1819) — treat these as one continuous record trail under different jurisdiction names.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records
- **Spanish Catholic registers (Mobile District, 1780–1813):** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and Spanish census returns.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — with copies at the **Library of Congress**.
- **Language:** Spanish (1780–1813); earlier French colonial records (1702–1763) are in French (originals at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives).
- FamilySearch also holds an **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** collection (ID 1986396, ~156,789 people), beginning within this period.

### Census Records
- **No surviving federal census** for this area in 1800 or 1810.
- **Mississippi Territory censuses:** 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama.
  - **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery (physical access).
- FamilySearch also holds **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (ID 2016756, ~287,634 people), covering the tail of this period.

### Probate and Court Records
- **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (FamilySearch collection ID 1537764, ~438,210 people) begins right at the edge of this period.
- FamilySearch digitized browse-only image volume: **Territorial court and land records, Alabama, 1808–1819** (imageGroupNumber 004512889, 214 images, 0% indexed — must be browsed page by page).

### Land Records
- **Spanish and British colonial land grants** in the Mobile area are the earliest surviving series.
  - Colonial grants held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Library of Congress.
- FamilySearch digitized browse-only image volume: **County deed and probate records, Washington, Alabama, 1803–1820** (imageGroupNumber 004512890, 96 images, 0% indexed — browse only).

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No civil vital registration** existed in the territory at this date. Church and sacramental registers, land/probate records, and territorial/federal censuses substitute.

### Marriage Records
- **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (FamilySearch collection ID 1598408, ~1,224,690 people) begins within this period.

### Military Records
- Relevant conflicts include the Creek War (1813–1814). Federal-era service and pension records generally held at **NARA**; no Alabama-specific territorial militia collection was confirmed by this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection / Coverage |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1803–1950 (ID 1986396); County Marriages 1809–1950 (ID 1598408); Probate Records 1809–1985 (ID 1537764); Census Substitutes 1810–1890 (ID 2016756) |
| FamilySearch (browse-only images) | Territorial court & land records 1808–1819 (img 004512889); Washington Co. deed/probate 1803–1820 (img 004512890) |
| NARA | Federal records (land, military, pension) — https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records — https://www.fold3.com/ |

### Physical Archives
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History** (Montgomery, AL) | Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish-era Mobile District church registers, census returns, and land grants (1780–1813) |

---

## Records NOT Online
The 1801–1810 Mississippi Territory censuses and the Spanish-era Mobile District church/colonial records are held in physical archives (Montgomery, Seville, Aix-en-Provence) with no indication they are digitized or name-searchable online. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes that exist for this period are **images only, 0% name-indexed**, and must be browsed page by page.

1. **Search all three jurisdiction names** — Mississippi Territory (pre-1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819), and Alabama (post-1819) — rather than only "Alabama."

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Post / Arkansas Region (pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period, c. 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Arkansas Post** was established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley. Spain controlled the territory from the **1763 Treaty of Paris** until it secretly ceded it back to France in 1800.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (now in Arkansas County) served as the civil and military hub under Spanish administration.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana, under the authority of New Orleans and ultimately the Captaincy General of Cuba.
- Arkansas was **not** an independent territory in this period — records may be filed under Louisiana or French colonial collections rather than "Arkansas."

## Boundary / Jurisdictional Changes
This is a succession of rulers over the same settlement, not a geographic split:
- **1686–1763:** French authority
- **1763–1800:** Spanish authority
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase → U.S. territorial administration

---

## Available Record Types

### Church (Sacramental) Records
- French Catholic missionaries maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s through the colonial period.
- A **digitized volume** was confirmed: **Image group 008814402** — "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)," 1763–1800, 64 images, in **Spanish**, hosted on FamilySearch.
  - ⚠️ **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image. Reading requires Spanish-language skills.
- Original registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock**; transcribed copies are at the **Arkansas History Commission**.

### Census Records (Padrones)
- Spanish administrators kept civil/military records including **censuses (padrones)** at the post.
- These are **not digitized or online** in this survey — they exist as physical holdings.

### Land Records
- **Land concessions** were issued under Spanish administration and survive as part of the colonial record set.
- Not digitized; held at the repositories listed below.

### Military Records
- Arkansas Post was a military installation; civil and military records were maintained, but no specific surviving military series was confirmed beyond general colonial administration documents.

### Probate / Court Records
- **Not confirmed** for this period by any source found in this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Image group **008814402** — Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), 1763–1800, 64 images | Browse-only; in Spanish; not indexed |

> **Note:** FamilySearch's indexed collections for Arkansas begin only in the 1800s (earliest: Compiled Census Substitutes 1819–1870). There are **no indexed FamilySearch collections** for the Spanish colonial period. The FamilySearch Catalog search also returned zero hits for "Arkansas Post Spanish colonial" — a cataloguing gap, not proof the records don't exist.

### Physical / Microfilm Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock | Transcribed registers; padrones; land concessions | Physical access |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Physical access |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records (censuses, land concessions, correspondence) | The original Spanish colonial custodian |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm copies of the above colonial-era records | Microfilm access |

---

## Records NOT Online
- The padrones (censuses) and land concessions are **physical holdings only** at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias, and the Library of Congress (microfilm).
- Only the sacramental register volume (image group 008814402) is digitized, and it is browse-only.

## Known Record Losses
No tool result in this survey confirmed the destruction or loss of any specific Spanish colonial Arkansas records.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Browse the FamilySearch digitized register:** Image group 008814402 has 64 images of Spanish-language sacramental records (1763–1800). Plan to browse them all, as they are not indexed.
2. **Search Louisiana colonial records too:** Because Arkansas Post fell under Spanish Louisiana, related records (administrative correspondence, broader census lists) may be filed under Louisiana or New Orleans colonial collections — not under "Arkansas."
3. **Check French-era records (pre-1763):** If the family may have arrived before 1763, look into French colonial Louisiana materials as well.
4. **Target the Archivo General de Indias directly:** This is the original custodian of Spanish colonial administrative and census records for the region; it is outside FamilySearch's holdings.
5. **Early American territorial records (post-1803):** Families present before 1800 often appear in early U.S. territorial records after the Louisiana Purchase — these can help confirm identities traced through the colonial materials.

---

*This survey covers the Arkansas Post area and surrounding region before 1800. The most accessible surviving records are the unindexed Spanish-language church registers now digitized on FamilySearch. Census lists and land concession records are known to exist but are physical-only holdings. Because "Arkansas" was not yet a separate territory, cast a wide net across Louisiana colonial collections when searching.*

## Jurisdiction Overview

Washington County (organized 1788) and Hamilton County (organized 1790) were the first two counties carved out of the Northwest Territory, and jurisdiction over any given 1790 event depends on exactly where it occurred and when county lines were drawn or redrawn. For events before those counties fully covered an area, records may be filed under the Northwest Territory generally. **Treat Northwest Territory records and the early Washington/Hamilton County series as one continuous research trail.**

- Two distinct land-grant systems operated side by side:

  - **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio, surveyed on a grid) — records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**

### Church Records

### Census Records

### Tax Records

### Probate, Court, Military, and Other Records

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriages 1789–2013; Tax Records 1800–1850; Church Records 1787–1950; Land Records 1787–1840 | Online (familysearch.org) |

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- California became a U.S. state in 1850, bypassing territorial status.
- The Gold Rush began January 24, 1848, at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, and drew roughly 300,000 migrants from the U.S. and abroad, producing a transient, heavily male population.
- **Key historical events:** statehood in 1850; the 1850 federal census was California's first and was only partially preserved — some county returns are missing.

## Boundary changes
Pre-1850, California was Spanish then Mexican territory; it entered the Union directly as a state in 1850 rather than passing through territorial status. Many counties were newly created in this period — check each county's own formation date before assuming modern boundaries applied.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **County-level birth recording** from 1850 — this is a county, not state, series.
- **What exists:** County births 1850–1919 and county marriages 1850–1952.
- **Where held:** County level; no statewide civil registration start date was confirmed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Franciscan mission records (baptisms, marriages, burials), 1769–1834.

### Church records
- Catholic missions under Franciscan friars predate statehood (1769–1834).
- **Record types:** baptisms, marriages, burials recorded by mission friars.
- The collection **"California, Mission Records, 1769-1850"** is indexed on FamilySearch (98,765 people).
- Mission-era registers are generally in Spanish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census was California's first, but was only *partially preserved* — some county returns are missing.
- **State census:** A "California State Census" covering 1850–1852 (88% name-indexed and full-text searchable) can partly substitute for missing federal county returns.

### Probate and court records
- Wills, inventories, administrations, guardianship files — held at the county or district courthouse level.
- No California-specific probate collection or date range was confirmed by this survey's tools; check both wills and administration series at the relevant county.

### Land records / Mining claims
- **Mining claims specifically:** A "Mining Claim Registers" volume for San Francisco, 1849–1855 — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- Mining claim registers were held at county recorder's offices.
- Federal land patents are accessible via the BLM/GLO website; Mexican-era land grants required confirmation through U.S. land commissions.

### Military records
No California-specific Gold Rush-era military record collections were confirmed by this survey's tools. General resources: service/pension/draft records at NARA; state adjutant general records at the California State Archives.

### Cemetery records
No California-specific cemetery collection was returned. **Find A Grave** is a curated external resource for burial records.

### Newspaper records
No California-specific newspaper collection was confirmed. **Newspapers.com** is a curated external resource for historical newspapers.

### Immigration / arrival records
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- San Francisco ship passenger manifests are held at the **National Archives, San Bruno**.
- Overland migrants may appear in trail diaries and journals rather than any official passenger list.

### Other record types
- **Voter registration (Great Registers):** "California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (1,345,678 people) — post-1860, so background only for the Gold Rush window.
- Manuscript collections: the **California State Library** and the **Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley** hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript material.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California, County Births, 1850-1919 (789,456 people) | County-level birth registration from 1850 |
| FamilySearch | California, County Marriages, 1850-1952 (1,135,780 people) | County marriage records |
| FamilySearch | California, Mission Records, 1769-1850 (98,765 people) | Pre-statehood vital events via mission registers |
| FamilySearch | California State Census, 1850-1852 (88% indexed) | Substitute for missing 1850 federal census counties |
| FamilySearch | Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849-1855 (browse-only) | Mining claim documentation |
| FamilySearch | Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849-1858 (browse-only) | Arrival records for sea migrants |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Supplements the partially-destroyed 1850 California census |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Burial locations |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Obituaries and legal notices |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records portal | Passenger manifests, naturalization records |
| Fold3 | Military records | Service/pension records |

### Physical repositories
- **California State Library** and **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** — extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections; no online catalog detail was retrieved in this survey — a direct inquiry is recommended.
- **National Archives, San Bruno** — San Francisco ship passenger manifests.

---

## Records NOT online (browse-only or unconfirmed)
- Mining claim registers (San Francisco, 1849–1855) — digitized but 0% indexed; must be browsed image by image.
- Port arrival registers (Sacramento, 1849–1858) — likewise browse-only.
- County-level probate, land, tax, and newspaper records were **not confirmed online** by this survey's tools.

## Known record losses
The 1850 federal census of California had some county returns lost or missing. The 1850–1852 California state census (88% indexed) is a partial substitute.

---

## Research tips

1. **Use the 1850–1852 California state census** to fill gaps where 1850 federal census county returns are missing — it is well-indexed and full-text searchable.
2. **Mining claim registers and port arrival registers are browse-only** — expect to browse by county/port and date rather than search by name.
3. **San Francisco ship passenger manifests** are at NARA San Bruno; overland migrants may appear in trail diaries and journals rather than official passenger lists.
4. **Pre-statehood vital events** (1769–1834) are recorded only in Franciscan mission registers, not in any civil series.
5. **California State Library and Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections worth a direct inquiry.
6. Many county-level records (probate, deeds, tax lists) exist only at **county recorder/courthouse level** — identify the specific county first, then contact that county's office or state archives.
7. This was a transient, heavily male population — many miners left no permanent record in California if they arrived, mined briefly, and departed. Cross-reference home-state records (birthplace, prior residence) alongside California sources.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700–1800, Colonial/Early Federal Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Origins:** New York City began as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (1626), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York. Records therefore span both a **Dutch colonial** (1626–1664) and **British colonial** (1664–1783) period.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches all kept extensive registers — these are the primary source of vital events for the 1700s.
- **Key transition:** New York became a U.S. state in 1788; the city briefly served as the first U.S. capital after the Revolution.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(Primary vital-event source for this era)*
- Civil registration did not exist in this period — **church registers are your main substitute for births, marriages, and deaths.**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776** — One digitized volume was found on FamilySearch (image group **007733180**, 211 images). **Important caveats:** it is **0% name-indexed**, is **browse-only** (no full-text search), and is written in **Dutch**. It must be read page by page; translation help will be needed.
- **Online collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (FamilySearch collection id **1469062**, ~2.3 million people) covers much of this period.
- **Not confirmed online:** Trinity/Anglican and Presbyterian registers for the 1700–1800 window did not appear as separate digitized volumes in this survey — treat those as leads requiring direct contact with physical repositories.

### Census Records
- Federal census records begin in **1790** — useful for the final decade of this period.
- No confirmed colonial-era New York City census was found for the 1700s; tax lists and militia rolls serve a similar purpose (see below).

### Probate Records
- Wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**. Abstracts are published by the **New-York Historical Society**.
- **Online collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (FamilySearch collection id **1542780**, ~988,000 people).

### Land Records
- **Online collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (FamilySearch collection id **2078654**, ~1.6 million people). Land patents during the colonial period were issued by the Province of New York.

### Tax & Military Records
- **Tax assessment lists** survive for some years and wards of colonial New York City. The online collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (FamilySearch collection id **1678432**) covers the tail end of this period.
- **Colonial militia rolls** list men of military age by ward — useful for locating residents. These are held at the **New York State Archives** (New York Colonial Manuscripts).

### Cemetery & Newspaper Records
- Find A Grave and Newspapers.com are available external resources, though no colonial-era NYC-specific digitized collection was confirmed in this survey.
- The *New York Gazette* is a known colonial-era paper, but no confirmed digitized date-range or repository was returned by tools.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collection | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 (id 1469062) | Baptisms, marriages, burials — primary vital substitute |
| FamilySearch | Dutch Reformed Church Registers, NYC, 1700–1776 (image group 007733180) | Browse-only, Dutch-language, unindexed |
| FamilySearch | New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 (id 1542780) | Wills and estate records |
| FamilySearch | New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 (id 2078654) | Deeds, land patents |
| FamilySearch | New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804 (id 1678432) | Identifying residents by ward |

### Physical Repositories
- **New York State Archives** — New York Colonial Manuscripts (militia rolls, tax lists, administrative records)
- **New-York Historical Society** — Published abstracts of wills proved before the Prerogative Court; extensive colonial-era collections
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** — Colonial-era research collections and published guides

---

## Records NOT Confirmed Online
- Trinity Church (Anglican) and Presbyterian church registers for this period
- Mayor's Court records
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (physical/archival at the State Archives)
- Pre-1790 census or population lists

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the Dutch Reformed registers.** The series is the oldest and most continuous for New York City (beginning 1639). The one digitized volume (1700–1776) requires page-by-page browsing in Dutch.
2. **Search tax and militia records** at the New York State Archives to locate male residents by ward and approximate age when vital records are absent.
3. **Wills are abstracted** in a New-York Historical Society publication series — consult that society directly, as no online digitization of that series was confirmed.
4. **Search by ward, not modern neighborhood.** Colonial-era parish, court, and tax records were organized by ward and parish boundaries that do not map neatly to later borough or neighborhood lines.
5. **FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits** for New York City in this survey — that is a cataloguing gap, not proof records are absent. Search the catalog directly by surname or record title.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki's "New York City Genealogy" page** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) is the best confirmed starting point for the colonial records section specifically.

---

**Summary:** The strongest confirmed online source for 1700s New York City families is the Dutch Reformed Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers — though the digitized set is unindexed and in Dutch. Tax lists, land records, and probate (will) records exist in FamilySearch's online collections and span this era. For Anglican/Trinity, Presbyterian, court, and newspaper records, direct contact with the New-York Historical Society, the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society, or the New York State Archives is the recommended next step.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Virginia transitioned from a British colony to a state in 1776, mid-war.
- County-level record-keeping dates to the 1630s, making Virginia one of the best-documented colonies.
- Virginia contributed more troops than any other colony/state; the decisive Siege of Yorktown (1781) was fought on Virginia soil.

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content during this survey, so wiki-sourced claims are noted where they come from leads rather than confirmed articles.

---

## Available Record Types

### Military Records
- **Continental Line service records & muster rolls** — National Archives, Record Group 93
- **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond (physical access; digitization status unconfirmed)
- **Pension & bounty-land warrant applications** — NARA, Record Group 15
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published (source: wiki_search lead)
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** *Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783* (collection id 1945678, ~345,678 persons, indexed)
- **Browse-only volume:** Image group 005301447 — Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (341 images, 0% indexed — must be browsed page by page)

### Land Records (Bounty Land)
- Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to Revolutionary veterans; warrant and survey records connect veterans to claims.
- Same browse-only volume (005301447) covers the bounty warrants.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (id 1734285, ~2.57 million persons, indexed)

### County Court & Tax Records
- **Tax lists as census substitute:** Because Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed (see "Record Losses" below), 1780s county tax lists are the primary census substitute for this period.
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - *Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850* (id 1456723, ~456,789 persons)
  - *Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920* (id 2134567, ~1.79 million persons)
- **Browse volume:** Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 — image group 005301448 (158 images, 61% name-indexed)
- **Full-text volume:** Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799 — image group 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable)

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929* (id 1598230, ~1.23 million persons)
- Specific denominations included were not confirmed in this survey.

### Probate Records
- Covered within *Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900* (id 1734285).

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Military 1775–1783; Land/Marriage/Will 1600–1900; Tax 1782–1850; Court 1650–1920; Church 1680–1929 | familysearch.org (free) |
| **Fold3** | Military service & pension records (NARA-sourced) | fold3.com (subscription) |
| **NARA** | Originals of RG 93 (service/muster) & RG 15 (pension/bounty-land) | archives.gov |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia records | Physical or written inquiry; digitization status unconfirmed |

---

## Records NOT Fully Online
- The 341-image bounty-warrant volume (005301447) is **not name-searchable** — browsed image by image only.
- Augusta County court order books (005301448) are only **61% indexed** — partial name search, rest requires browsing.
- Library of Virginia militia holdings: treat as **physical-access-only** until confirmed otherwise.

---

## Known Record Losses
- **Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from the 1780s are the documented genealogical substitute.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Search both** Continental Line (NARA RG 93) and Virginia militia (Library of Virginia) records — soldiers commonly served in both over the course of the war.
2. **Use 1780s tax lists** as your primary stand-in for the missing 1790 census.
3. If your ancestor claimed **Ohio bounty land**, plan to browse image group 005301447 page by page, as it is unindexed.
4. **Narrow to a county** if possible — Virginia's county records are unusually well preserved, and knowing the county opens additional deed, court, and church records.
5. For pension files, the **Fold3 / NARA pension applications** often contain biographical narratives, depositions, and widow's applications with family details well beyond mere service dates.

Virginia maintained county-level record-keeping from the 1630s.

## Boundary changes
This survey did not confirm specific county boundary changes for 1775-1783; county jurisdiction in colonial/Revolutionary Virginia was fluid (new counties were regularly split off), so if you narrow to a specific county, check that county's formation date before assuming records are filed there rather than under its parent county.

## Available record types

### Military records
- **What exists:** A wiki_search hit (not a full page fetch, so treated as a lead, not a confirmed page) names: Continental Line service records and muster rolls at the National Archives (Record Group 93); Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia in Richmond; pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15); published Virginia State Navy records.

### Land records (bounty land)
- **What exists:** Virginia granted bounty lands to Revolutionary veterans in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (per the wiki_search lead); warrant and survey records connect veterans to claims.
- **Digitized:** The same browse-only image group (005301447) above covers the bounty warrants themselves, 1779-1800.
- **Other land/deed records:** `collections_search` also returned "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (id 1734285, ~2.57 million persons), indexed.

### County court and tax records
- **Court order books:** `volume_search` found image group 005301448 — Augusta County, Virginia court order books, 1775-1795, 158 images, 61% name-indexed (not full-text) — partially searchable by name.
- **Tax lists as census substitute:** A wiki_search result states county tax lists from the 1780s are among the earliest substitutes for the 1790 Virginia federal census, which was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. `volume_search` also returned image group 005301449 — Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782-1799, 87 images, full-text searchable (not name-indexed).
- **Digitized collection:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (id 1456723, ~456,789 persons) and "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (id 2134567, ~1.79 million persons), both from `collections_search`.

### Church records
- **Digitized collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (id 1598230, ~1.23 million persons) from `collections_search`, spanning the Revolutionary period.
- This survey did not confirm which specific denominations' registers are included, since the fetched FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content rather than a Virginia-specific article.

### Census records
- No 1775-1783 federal or state census exists (the first federal census was 1790, and Virginia's 1790 schedule was destroyed in 1814 per the record above). County tax lists (above) are the documented substitute for this gap.

### Probate records
- Covered within "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (id 1734285) per `collections_search`; this survey found no period-specific probate collection beyond that.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (id 1945678); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (id 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (id 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (id 2134567); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (id 1598230) | name-indexed access to military, land, tax, court and church records | not stated |
| Fold3 | Military records (per external_links_search) | NARA-style military service/pension record access | not stated |
| NARA | archives.gov — originals of Continental Line service, pension and bounty-land files | source of RG 93 and RG 15 records | not stated |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes total for 1775-1783 military/land/tax record types (image groups 005301447, 005301448, 005301449); this appears to be the complete result set for the query run (no `nextPageToken` returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Virginia militia records, per the wiki_search lead | Not stated by this survey — visit or write to the repository |

This survey named no other physical repository beyond the Library of Virginia lead above.

## Records NOT online
The 341-image bounty-warrant volume (005301447) and most of the 158-image Augusta County court order books (005301448, only 61% indexed) are not browsable by name search online in full; a researcher must page through images directly. County tax lists from the 1780s (image group 005301449, and the "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" collection) are the documented substitute. No other record loss was confirmed by this survey.

## Research tips

---
This survey covered Virginia statewide for the Revolutionary War years 1775 to 1783, since no single county was named. Virginia kept unusually good colonial county records, and for this war period the most useful sources are militia and Continental Army service and pension files (held by the National Archives and, for militia, the Library of Virginia), bounty-land warrant records tied to Ohio land grants given to veterans, and 1780s county tax lists, which genealogists use in place of the 1790 census because it was destroyed by fire in 1814; some of these records are only browsable page-by-page online rather than searchable by name, and a few leads (Library of Virginia holdings, Virginia's own research wiki page) could not be fully confirmed in this pass. The locality guide for New Orleans (Orleans Parish, Louisiana, 1790–1820) has been saved to your project. Here is what it found regarding record survival and substitutes:

---

## Disasters and Record Survival in Early 1800s New Orleans

**What was lost:**
New Orleans suffered two catastrophic fires — in **1788 and 1794** — that destroyed most of the French Quarter and wiped out much of the colonial paper trail. Later hurricanes, floods, and yellow fever outbreaks caused further archival damage over the years.

**What survived — and where to look:**

1. **Catholic Sacramental Registers (St. Louis Cathedral)**
   - Baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded from **1731 onward**.
   - Gaps correspond to the fire years, but losses were partial — not total.
   - These registers substitute directly for vital records that would not exist as civil documents until later.

2. **Notarial Records (New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center)**
   - New Orleans operated under **civil law**, meaning notaries — rather than courthouses — handled property, contracts, wills, estate inventories, and family agreements.
   - Over **30 million pages** survive, dating back to 1734; a microfilm reel covering **1803–1820** has been digitized (though unindexed).
   - These records substitute for the probate, deed, and estate records you would typically find in an English-law county courthouse elsewhere in the U.S.

**Caveats:**
The guide notes it could not confirm precise access details for the church registers or the Notarial Archives from the Wiki pages consulted, as some returned generic rather than place-specific guidance.

**Recommended next steps:**
- Contact the **Archdiocese of New Orleans archives** directly for sacramental register access.
- Contact the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** for the notarial microfilm.
- Consider re-running searches against the FamilySearch Wiki for more detailed guidance on accessing these substitutes before building a full research plan.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Founded:** New Orleans founded 1718 by the French; passed to Spain 1763, briefly back to France, then to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 (Wikipedia, "New Orleans").
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory/State (statehood 1812); the city sits in Orleans Parish, Louisiana's parish-based civil-law system (Napoleonic Code), not the county system used elsewhere in the US (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "Louisiana Genealogy" #Parish_System).
- **Legal system note:** Because Louisiana is a civil-law jurisdiction, notarial acts are a central legal record series (unlike common-law states) and successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship) and interdictions are the Louisiana-specific equivalents of other states' probate/guardianship records (same source).
- **Key historical events bearing on records:** major fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial French Quarter and many early records; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further damage to archival holdings over time (Wikipedia, "New Orleans"; FamilySearch Wiki search index, "New Orleans Genealogy" #Records_Surviving_Disasters).

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** This survey did not confirm a FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Vital_Records page giving a specific statewide start year; the only dated statewide collection returned is "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964" (collection 1543892, collections_search), suggesting some statewide death indexing from 1819, but the registration level and date are not confirmed by a Wiki page.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** For 1790-1820, sacramental (church) registers are the primary substitute — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (the dominant faith under French/Spanish rule).
- **Record types / survival:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral record baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, "though with gaps" — these gaps align with the 1788 and 1794 fires (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "New Orleans Genealogy" #Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Where held:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey (the index excerpt names the registers but not a specific repository/access point); confirm directly with the Archdiocese of New Orleans or its archives before relying on this guide alone.

### Court and notarial records
- **Notarial acts:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 — a uniquely Louisiana civil-law record series that substitutes for many deed, contract, and family-related records found elsewhere in probate or land offices (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "New Orleans Genealogy" #Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Cabildo records:** Records of the Cabildo, the Spanish colonial governing body, are named by the same source as a surviving genealogical source for the colonial period, though no tool result in this survey gives their current repository or access method.
- **Digitized holdings found:** volume_search returned one microfilm volume group (image group 004990115, 167 images) covering "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)" for Orleans, Louisiana, 1803-1820, in French and English, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.

### Probate and succession records
- **Types:** Louisiana's civil-law probate equivalents are successions (not "probate"/"wills" in the common-law sense), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "Louisiana Genealogy" #Parish_System).
- **Digitized collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, collections_search), indexed with 456,789 linked persons — date range covers the 1790-1820 target period.
- **Where held:** Not stated beyond the FamilySearch collection; this survey found no catalog_search hit for Orleans Parish probate originals (catalog_search returned 0 hits for this place).

### Census records

- **Access:** Not independently confirmed for this place/period by collections_search or volume_search.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey — no Louisiana_Land_and_Property page content was returned (the direct wiki_read fell back to a generic page).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Port:** New Orleans was a major port of entry; no specific passenger-list collection for this place/period was returned by collections_search or volume_search in this survey.

### Other

## Research tips
- Because the 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed much of the colonial built environment and many records, do not expect a continuous civil paper trail before the early 1800s — rely on sacramental registers and notarial acts, which are reported to survive with gaps rather than being wholly lost (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "New Orleans Genealogy" #Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Search notarial acts as a primary record class for this place and period, not a secondary one — Louisiana's civil-law system routed family, property, and contract matters through notaries far more than courthouses in common-law states (same source).
- When looking for "probate," search instead for successions, tutorships, and interdictions, the Louisiana civil-law terms for probate, guardianship, and related proceedings (FamilySearch Wiki search index, "Louisiana Genealogy" #Parish_System).
- The one digitized notarial-acts volume found for this period (1803-1820) is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable, so it must be browsed image by image, and it is partly in French — be prepared to read French-language entries.
- Several FamilySearch Wiki pages that would normally anchor this guide (Louisiana_Vital_Records, New_Orleans_Genealogy, Louisiana_Genealogy, and all four place-page sections) returned only generic fallback content when fetched directly in this survey; re-run this guide later or consult the Wiki directly, since the disaster/notarial detail above came only from a search-index excerpt, not a full page read.
- Confirm directly with the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives and the Notarial Archives Research Center for access procedures, since no tool result in this survey gave repository contact or access details for either.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — 1840s Port of Entry

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston in the 1840s was one of America's busiest immigrant ports, receiving especially large numbers of Irish fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Core Record Type: Passenger/Arrival Lists

- **What exists:** U.S. Customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston, 1820–1891, held in National Archives Record Group 36.
- **1840s coverage:** 1840s customs lists typically record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — later manifests include more detail (last residence, destination).
- **Digitized volume found:** Image group **003345210**, "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1840–1850 (389 images). Only **3% name-indexed** — must be searched via **full-text search** or browsed page-by-page; don't rely on the name index.
- **Broader indexed collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection id **1784312**) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312
- **Physical originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA).

> **Tip:** Search the full-text-searchable volume (003345210) directly on FamilySearch, since the name index covers only 3% of images.

---

## Supporting Record Types

### Church Records
- Catholic parish registers — especially Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's — document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s.
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (id **1921657**) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Physical originals:** Archdiocese of Boston archives.
- **Value:** Especially useful since many 1840s arrivals predate comprehensive civil vital registration — baptism/marriage entries can substitute for missing vital records.

### Naturalization Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (id **1459213**) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213
- **Important:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record (federal, state, or local) — search broadly across Massachusetts courts, not just Boston.

### Civil Vital Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (id **2061550**) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550

### Probate Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (id **1678901**) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901

### Newspapers — *The Pilot*
- *The Pilot*, an Irish Catholic newspaper published in Boston, ran **arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements** for Irish immigrants during this era. This is a particularly notable finding aid for tracing Famine-era arrivals and reconnecting separated families.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (online) | Boston passenger-list volume 003345210 (full-text); broader MA Passenger Lists coll. 1784312; Church, Naturalization, Vital, Probate collections | familysearch.org |
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original RG 36 customs manifests | Physical / archives.gov |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Physical / contact required |
| Newspapers.com / other newspaper sites | *The Pilot* arrival notices, obituaries | Subscription |

---

## Key Tips for 1840s Boston Research

1. **Full-text search first** on FamilySearch volume 003345210 — the name index is nearly empty.
2. **Check *The Pilot*** for arrival and "looking for lost relatives" notices, especially for Irish Famine-era immigrants.
3. **Search Catholic parish registers** (via Archdiocese of Boston archives and FamilySearch collection 1921657) for baptisms and marriages that anchor an immigrant's early years in Boston.
4. **Cast a wide net for naturalizations** — the petition may be in any Massachusetts court, not just a Boston-area court.
5. The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for "passenger lists" at Boston — this is a **cataloguing gap**, not an absence of records; rely on the collections and volumes identified above.

---

If you'd like, I can turn these leads into a step-by-step research plan with specific searches to run first.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma / Indian Territory (Mid-1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Indian Territory was federally administered land set aside for relocated Native American nations under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. The Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were relocated there via the Trail of Tears. Oklahoma did not become a state until 1907; for mid-1800s research you are entirely in a tribal-nation and federal-agency framework, **not** a county system.

---

## Key Record Types & Collections

### 🏛️ Tribal Rolls and Censuses
The most essential sources for this period:
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** and **Drennen Roll (1852)** — mid-1800s tribal enrollment records (FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — name, age, sex, blood quantum, tribal affiliation; held at NARA Fort Worth, indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"* (collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people) — begins right at the mid-1800s window
- **Digitized Volume:** Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870 (image group 002298871, 940 images) — 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch

### 📜 Treaty & Federal Agency Records
- Bureau of Indian Affairs annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and school records
- Held at the **National Archives at Fort Worth** (the primary physical repository for these)
- Treaty documents themselves are federal records at NARA — not digitized in a searchable collection; require direct archival access
- More info: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records

### ⛪ Church / Mission Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"* (collection id 1654321, ~123,456 people)
- Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students, and community members from the 1820s onward — these are the practical substitute for civil vital registration, which did not exist

### 🗺️ Land Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"* (collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people) — covers the full mid-1800s window
- Note: Tribal allotment/land-assignment systems operated differently from the standard federal rectangular-survey system; individual tribal-nation land offices governed assignments

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Tribal rolls (1851–1959), land records (1834–1907), mission/church records (1820–1965), enrollment-card volume (1840–1870) | Free online |
| **National Archives, Fort Worth** | Dawes Rolls, BIA agency/annuity records, treaty documents | In person or NARA request; https://www.archives.gov/ |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes-era roll indexes, federal censuses | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service and pension records | Subscription; https://www.fold3.com/ |

---

## Important Research Notes

1. **No county system in mid-1800s.** Use tribal-nation affiliation as your primary organizing structure — not county of residence. Counties only appeared with Oklahoma Territory's organization in 1890 and statehood in 1907.

2. **No standard civil vital registration.** Mission and church registers plus tribal enrollment rolls are the practical substitutes for birth, marriage, and death records in this era.

3. **Federal census gaps.** The federal decennial census did not enumerate Indian Territory residents by name in the standard way during this period. Use tribal rolls as the enumeration equivalent.

4. **Start with the rolls, then work forward.** Begin with the 1851 Old Settler Cherokee Roll and 1852 Drennen Roll as mid-1800s enrollment sources, then trace families forward to the Dawes Rolls for continuity.

5. **Tribal court and probate records** are not confirmed as digitized by this survey — expect physical/archival research at NARA for those materials.

---

## Suggested Research Path
1. Search the **1840–1870 Tribal Enrollment Cards** volume on FamilySearch (image group 002298871) — fully indexed and searchable
2. Check the **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** collection (id 1987432)
3. Search **Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** (id 1654321) for baptisms, marriages, and deaths
4. Contact **NARA Fort Worth** for BIA agency/annuity payment rolls and treaty-implementation documents
5. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records for tribe-specific sub-pages (Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, etc.)

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma / Indian Territory, United States (mid-1800s, focus on Five Civilized Tribes)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status in period:** Indian Territory was land set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for forced relocation of Native American tribes; the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) were relocated there via the Trail of Tears (Wikipedia, "Oklahoma").
- **Statehood:** Oklahoma did not become a state until 1907 — for the mid-1800s window you are working entirely within federally administered Indian Territory, not a state or county system.
- Population figures and a dedicated FamilySearch county/state research-guide page could not be confirmed in this survey — several lookups for "Oklahoma, United States" and "Indian Territory, United States" returned only a generic, non-place-specific FamilySearch Wiki template rather than content for this place. Treat this as a tool/coverage gap, not evidence that no such page exists.

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory was not organized as counties in the mid-1800s; it was divided among tribal nations' own jurisdictions (Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, Chickasaw Nation, Creek/Muscogee Nation, Seminole Nation), each with its own governing institutions. Present-day Oklahoma counties were not created until the 1890 Oklahoma Territory organization and 1907 statehood, so mid-1800s records are filed under tribal-nation and federal-agency names, not county names.

## Available record types

### Tribal rolls and censuses
- **What exists:** A FamilySearch Wiki search result ("Oklahoma Native American Records," Tribal Rolls section) names the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) as mid-1800s-era tribal enrollment records, plus the later Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) which record name, age, sex, blood quantum and tribal affiliation (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people) — date range begins exactly in the mid-1800s window (collections_search).
- **Digitized volume:** one volume found covering Indian Territory, 1840-1870, "Tribal Enrollment Cards," image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable (volume_search) — classify as **indexed + images**.
- **Where held:** per the wiki search result, the Dawes Rolls and related allotment records are held at the National Archives at Fort Worth, with online indexes at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Treaty and federal agency records
- **What exists:** Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records — annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records — are described in the wiki search result ("Oklahoma Native American Records," Missionary and Agency Records section) as held at the National Archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- **Treaties themselves** (the Indian Removal–era treaties with each of the Five Tribes) are federal documents held at the National Archives; this survey did not turn up a specific digitized treaty-text collection, only the agency/annuity records that implemented them — treat treaty document access as a NARA research task rather than a FamilySearch-indexed one.

### Church/mission records
- **What exists:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection id 1654321, ~123,456 people) spans the mid-1800s (collections_search). The wiki search result adds that Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries kept registers of converts, students and community members among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward.
- **Where held:** denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm, per the same result; no specific repository address was returned by this survey.

### Land records
- **What exists:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people) covers the full mid-1800s period (collections_search).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** tribal allotment and land-assignment systems operated differently from the federal rectangular-survey/BLM system used elsewhere; this survey did not confirm which office administered mid-1800s tribal land assignments — treat that as unconfirmed rather than assume a standard BLM General Land Office patent process applied.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Civil registration as a county/state system did not exist in Indian Territory in the mid-1800s (no counties existed yet). This survey's attempts to fetch a jurisdiction-specific Vital Records page returned only generic FamilySearch Wiki boilerplate, not Oklahoma-specific content, so no registration start date can be given — do not assume one. Tribal rolls and mission/church registers are the practical substitute for this period.

### Census records
- No Oklahoma/Indian Territory state or territorial census was confirmed by this survey; the federal decennial census did not enumerate Indian Territory residents by name in the standard way during this period. The tribal rolls/censuses above are the relevant enumeration substitute.

### Probate, court, military, immigration, tax, cemetery, newspaper records
- No tool result in this survey returned place-specific data for these categories for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s (catalog_search returned 0 hits; collections_search returned only the four collections listed above). Report this as a coverage gap in this survey, not as evidence these records don't exist — tribal nations maintained their own court and probate systems, and federal military/pension files exist for some tribal members (e.g., Civil War-era service), but none of that was confirmed here.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (id 1987432); "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (id 1541872); "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (id 1654321) | tribal rolls, land assignments, church/mission registers | not stated |
| FamilySearch (digitized volume) | Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840-1870 (image group 002298871) | indexed, full-text searchable enrollment images | not stated |

| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection link (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | general census access; wiki search result also names Ancestry as an index host for Dawes-era rolls | not stated |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | military records | not stated |

**Coverage of this survey:** only one digitized volume was returned by volume_search for this place/period (1840-1870); this is the full result set returned, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records (per wiki search result) | in person / NARA request |

## Records NOT online
- Treaty texts themselves, tribal-nation court and probate proceedings, and most mid-1800s BIA agency correspondence were not found digitized or indexed by this survey's tools — expect physical/archival research at NARA (Fort Worth and Washington, D.C. facilities) for these.

## Known record losses
- This survey's tools did not report any specific record loss (fire, destruction) for Indian Territory tribal or agency records in this period. Do not assume loss; the gaps above reflect digitization/indexing status, not destruction, except where stated.

## Research tips
- Start with the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) as mid-1800s tribal enrollment sources, then work forward to the later Dawes Rolls for continuity of family lines (FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- Search mission and church registers (1820-1965 collection) for baptisms and births that predate any civil recordkeeping — missionaries were often the only record-keepers in Indian Territory during this period.
- Because this survey could not retrieve a jurisdiction-specific FamilySearch Wiki research-strategy page for Oklahoma/Indian Territory (the tool returned only generic boilerplate), supplement this guide by consulting the FamilySearch Wiki site directly for an "Oklahoma Native American Records" or tribe-specific page, and the National Archives' Fort Worth facility finding aids for BIA records.
- Treat tribal-nation affiliation and rolls membership as the primary identifying structure for this period rather than county of residence, since no county system existed yet.

---
This survey looked at Oklahoma while it was still called Indian Territory, covering roughly the 1830s through 1870s, focusing on the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations relocated there. The most useful mid-1800s sources are the tribal enrollment and census rolls (such as the 1851 Old Settler Cherokee Roll and 1852 Drennen Roll, and a related 1840-1870 enrollment-card record set that is fully searchable online), along with mission and church registers kept by Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries, and land records covering 1834-1907; the treaty documents and day-to-day tribal government/agency records themselves are mostly only available by visiting or writing to the National Archives, particularly its Fort Worth facility, since no civil county system existed in the territory at that time. A few standard lookups (a general vital-records page and a general county/state research guide) did not return place-specific information in this pass, so some gaps noted above may simply be missing data from this particular search rather than records that don't exist. Next, a research plan can be built around searching the named tribal rolls and the digitized enrollment-card volume first, then following up with the National Archives for treaty and agency documents.

Here is what the locality-guide found for Pennsylvania Quaker families in the late 1700s:

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Records — Late 1700s**

The key records for this period are **not** government records but the Quakers' own **meeting records**, which substitute entirely for civil registration (Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration until 1906). These include:

- **Monthly, quarterly, and yearly meeting minutes** — detailed logs of births, marriages, deaths, memberships
- **Certificates of removal** — transfer records when a family moved from one meeting to another (invaluable for tracking migrations)
- **Disownment records** — disciplinary actions, which can document individuals who left the faith

**Key Geographic Areas:** Quaker communities were densest in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties.

---

**Where to Find Them**

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | Major archive of original Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records |
| **Quaker & Special Collections, Haverford College** | Another primary repository for original minutes and registers |
| **FamilySearch** | At least one digitized (but *unindexed*) Philadelphia Yearly Meeting volume, 1750–1800 (~145 images) — must be browsed page by page |
| **Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 vols.)** | Published abstracts of meeting records; useful where originals are not digitized |

---

**Research Tips**
- Because Quakers were disowned for marrying outside the faith, the **absence** of a marriage record in meeting minutes may itself be significant.
- Certificates of removal follow families between meetings — search the destination meeting's records, not just the origin.
- This locality guide has been saved to your project (as `loc_001`). You can follow up with a **research plan** to build a staged search strategy from it.

> ⚠️ *Note: Some FamilySearch Wiki pages for general Pennsylvania did not return full detail during the search. Population figures, land-office jurisdiction, and tax/military record specifics may be documented there and are worth checking directly.*

Here is what the locality-guide found and recorded (saved as **loc_001** in your project):

---

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories

The 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed roughly one-tenth of Philadelphia's population between August and November. Because Pennsylvania had **no statewide vital registration system** at that time, the records that survive are scattered across several sources and repositories:

### Key Record Types

1. **Church Burial Registers** — The most important resource. Individual congregations kept their own burial books; notable ones include:
   - **Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal)** — one of the largest congregations in the city
   - **Gloria Dei "Old Swedes'" Church** — one of the oldest churches in Pennsylvania
   - Many other denominational churches (Catholic, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker) maintained separate registers

2. **Mathew Carey's Published Death List** — Carey compiled and published a list of the dead during and immediately after the epidemic (*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever*, 1793). This is a named-individual source and highly valuable for tracing epidemic victims.

3. **Citizens' Relief Committee Minutes** — The volunteer relief organization kept meeting minutes that may name individuals who received aid, died, or were orphaned.

4. **Bush Hill Fever Hospital Records** — Bush Hill was converted into a hospital for fever patients. Records related to this facility may survive in manuscript collections.

5. **Quaker Meeting Records** — A Quaker congregation volume from this era has been digitized but is **unindexed** (page-by-page browse only, no name search).

---

### Repositories to Check

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscript collections, Carey materials, committee records, church registers |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Municipal and civic records from the period |
| **FamilySearch (via church register microfilm)** | Digitized church registers — some indexed, some browse-only |
| **Christ Church Archives** | Original burial registers |
| **Gloria Dei Church** | Original Swedish Lutheran registers |

---

### Research Notes

- Pennsylvania did **not** require civil registration of deaths in 1793; church records are the primary substitute.
- The Mathew Carey death list is a good first stop — it is a **contemporary, named list** of victims.
- Some FamilySearch guide pages for this area were not fully responsive during this survey; it's worth checking the [FamilySearch Pennsylvania Research Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy) directly for updated collection links.
- For unindexed volumes (like the Quaker register), use the **search-images** agent to browse page by page.

---

**Suggested next step:** Use the **research-plan** agent with this locality guide (loc_001) to build a concrete, sequenced search plan for your specific ancestor.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871

## Jurisdiction & The Disaster

**Cook County, Illinois; county seat: Chicago.** The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, and left over 100,000 homeless. Crucially for genealogists, it **destroyed the Cook County Courthouse**, taking with it deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls. In response, the **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register destroyed deeds, creating a reconstructed property-record series.

---

## Record Losses

The fire destroyed:
- Pre-fire Cook County courthouse deeds and probate files
- Early birth, death, and marriage registers
- Many church registers (varying by parish — some survived or were re-established)

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records
- **Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** — FamilySearch collection id 2024189 (post-fire; civil registration effectively restarts here)
- **Death Records, 1871–1947** — FamilySearch collection id 1913456
- **Marriage Records, 1871–1920** — FamilySearch collection id 1756321
- Pre-1871 civil registration was not confirmed; church registers are the main substitute.

### Church Records
- **Chicago Church Records, 1833–1925** — FamilySearch collection id 1803978 (spans both sides of the fire; key substitute for lost vital records)
- Availability varies by parish; some registers were also destroyed.
- **Catholic parishes:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds surviving parish registers.

### Census Records
- The **1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses** for Chicago survived — the 1870 originals were kept in Washington, D.C., and were unaffected by the local fire. These are your best pre-fire population records.

### Probate & Court Records
- Pre-fire originals largely destroyed; a **reconstructed copies volume** (imageGroupNumber 009982110, 1865–1871, 38 images) exists on FamilySearch as **browse-only** (not indexed).
- **Post-fire property re-recordings** (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 1871–1880, 112 images) — 41% name-searchable; partially indexed, partially browse-only. Research both together as a continuous trail.

### Land Records
- The Burnt Record Act re-recordings (the 1871–1880 volume above) are the reconstructed deeds.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records**, held at the **Chicago History Museum**, are a critical substitute for pre-fire property ownership — a derivative source where originals no longer exist.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | Chicago city directories (1840s onward, survived the fire), maps, manuscripts |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance-company property records, photographs, personal papers |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (Northeastern Illinois University)** | Cook County records from 1871 onward |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward |
| **FamilySearch** | Microfilmed post-fire Cook County records |

---

## Research Strategy for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it predates the fire by one year and the originals survived intact. It places families in specific wards and can confirm household composition before the disaster.
2. **Use city directories** (Newberry Library) as a year-by-year substitute for missing vital records — they can confirm residence, occupation, and survival after the fire.
3. **Search the reconstructed court-record volumes** (imageGroupNumbers 009982110 and 009982111) together as a paired record trail, not separately.
4. **Check church registers** — especially at the Bernardin Archives for Catholic families — since some parish registers survived or were reconstructed independently.
5. **Chicago Title and Trust insurance abstracts** at the Chicago History Museum can establish pre-fire property ownership even where the original courthouse deeds are gone.
6. **Birth, death, and marriage registration restarts in 1871** — if an ancestor died or married after the fire, the county records should exist; before October 1871, turn to church registers and census as substitutes.

---

> **Tip:** The FamilySearch Wiki page "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy" is the recommended next stop for a full county-level survey, as it carries confirmed, specific content on surviving and reconstructed records that the general template pages do not.

---

*No project file was specified, so this guide was not saved to a project. If you'd like, I can save it inside a research project, narrow in on one record type (such as the church registers or insurance abstracts), or build a sequenced record-search plan from here.*

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **French Louisiana** was founded by La Salle's 1682 claim to the Mississippi basin; New Orleans founded 1718. France governed 1699–1762, then ceded territory to Spain (west) and Britain (east) in 1762–63, briefly regained it 1800–1803, then sold it to the US via the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Administrative body:** The **Superior Council** (*Conseil Supérieur*) handled land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories.
- **Religion:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church; the *Code Noir* required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons.
- **Key note:** Sovereignty shifted France → Spain (1762) → France (1800) → USA (1803). The same Catholic and notarial record series continued *across* these transitions — do not stop searching at a political boundary date.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church (Sacramental) Records
- **Types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — the only civil-vital-record substitute for this era.
- **St. Louis Cathedral** (New Orleans) holds registers from **1720**.
- Registers include enslaved and free people of color (Code Noir baptism requirement).
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 people) — search here first for a name hit.
- **FamilySearch browse-only images:** Image group 004330991 (Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers, 1720–1803, 264 images) — **not name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be browsed image by image. Written in **French and Spanish**.

### Superior Council Records (Court & Notarial)
- **Types:** Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories.
- **FamilySearch browse-only images:** Image group 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769, 149 images) — **not indexed**, in French/Spanish.
- **Physical originals:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans (partially digitized).

### Notarial Archives (1730s onward)
- **Types:** Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — oldest continuous notarial office in North America; public access, physical visit.

### Land Records
- French *concessions* and Spanish land grants (not English common-law deeds).
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (published text); **Louisiana State Land Office**.
- FamilySearch Wiki: "Louisiana Land and Property" covers colonial grants.

### Probate Records
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, ~456,789 people) — begins within this target period.
- Earlier estate inventories may also appear in the Superior Council records.

### Colonial Census / Population Rolls
- No US federal census existed before 1790, and Louisiana was not US territory until 1803.
- French-era census rolls and administrative correspondence are held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — an overseas physical repository.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection / Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (coll. 1612905) | Indexed; best first stop |
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (coll. 2078341) | Indexed |
| FamilySearch (images) | Sacramental registers, 1720–1803 (img. 004330991) | Browse-only; French/Spanish |
| FamilySearch (images) | Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769 (img. 004330992) | Browse-only; French/Spanish |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (court, land, estate inventories); partially digitized |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Contracts, wills, marriage settlements from 1730s onward |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Colonial administrative correspondence and census rolls |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French/Spanish-era land grant records |

---

## Records NOT Online
- The bulk of the Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center are **not fully digitized**.
- ANOM administrative records and colonial census rolls are in France with **no confirmed online digitization** from this survey.
- New Orleans Notarial Archives are accessible only in person.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Search both Catholic registers and Superior Council records together** — these are the two primary genealogical sources for this colony.
2. **Language:** The sacramental registers and notarial acts are in French and Spanish — plan to read (or have translated) the original-language entries.
3. **Don't stop at sovereignty boundaries** — the same record series continued across the 1762 and 1803 transitions.
4. **For land:** Start with the *American State Papers: Public Lands* and the Louisiana State Land Office, not county recorder offices — French/Spanish-era transactions used concessions and grants, not US-style deeds.
5. **For families with enslaved ancestors:** The *Code Noir* requirement means Catholic parish registers are a key source, as baptism records document enslaved and free people of color.
6. A research plan targeting a specific ancestor, parish, or post (Orleans, Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, etc.) will surface more targeted collections than this general state-level survey.
