# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana was founded by La Salle's 1682 claim to the Mississippi basin; New Orleans founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville (per Wikipedia, "French Louisiana"). France governed 1699-1762, ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain and the east to Britain in 1762-1763, then regained it briefly 1800-1803 before the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Administrative/record-keeping body:** the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) handled land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Religion:** the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana; the Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons (same page).
- **Key historical note:** sovereignty changed hands repeatedly (France to Spain, 1762; Spain to France, 1800; France to the US, 1803) — records from this single population can be filed under French, Spanish, or early American administration depending on the exact year.

## Boundary changes
This is a sovereignty change, not a county-boundary change: the same territory and the same record-creating institutions (Superior Council, Catholic parishes) continued operating across the 1762-1763 and 1800-1803 transfers. Records for a family present throughout should be searched continuously across these regimes rather than treated as separate jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic only (state-established); the St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds registers from 1720 (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy").
- **Record types:** baptisms, marriages, burials; Code Noir required baptism of enslaved persons, so parish registers also document enslaved and free people of color.
- **Where held:** a digitized volume set, "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans," image group 004330991, covers Orleans, Louisiana, 1720-1803 (264 images). `recordSearchablePercent` is 0 and `fulltextSearchable` is false — **browse-only, no name index**, and the registers are in **French and Spanish** (languages: fr, es), so the researcher must read the original language. A separate indexed collection, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (FamilySearch collection 1612905, ~987,654 people), overlaps this period and should be searched first for a name hit before falling back to browsing the sacramental-register images.
- **Gaps:** no FamilySearch Wiki page specific to Louisiana church records was retrievable in this survey (see Research tips below) — denomination-by-denomination survival outside New Orleans was not confirmed.

### Court and notarial records (Superior Council)
- **Types:** land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy").
- **Where held:** the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, holds these partially digitized (same page). A digitized, browse-only volume, "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," image group 004330992, covers Louisiana, 1699-1769 (149 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, languages fr/es).
- **Administrative correspondence/census rolls:** the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, holds these for the colony (same page) — a physical-only, overseas repository for this material.

### Notarial archives (post-1730s)
- **Types:** contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions, from the 1730s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Where held:** the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, described as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, provides public access (same page) — a physical repository.

### Land records
- **Survey system / land-distribution jurisdiction:** French concessions and later Spanish land grants, not English common-law deeds; documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office (same page).
- **Types:** concessions (French-era grants), Spanish land grants, deeds via the notarial archives above.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; American State Papers series (published, so may be findable in libraries/online text repositories — not separately confirmed by this survey).

### Probate records
- **Date range:** the indexed collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (FamilySearch collection 2078341, ~456,789 people) begins within the target period.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed); earlier estate inventories may also appear among the Superior Council records above.
- **Testate/intestate:** not distinguished by any tool result in this survey — search both wills and administrations.

### Census / population counts
- This survey's `place_population` call returned no data for Louisiana/1700-1803; colonial population figures are not confirmed by any tool result here. The Wikipedia summary ("French Louisiana") gives founding/administrative facts but no population figures. Researchers should expect colonial-era counts (if any) to come from ANOM-held French census rolls, not a US federal census (which did not exist before 1790 and did not cover French/Spanish Louisiana during this window).

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No state-level civil registration existed in this period; the Catholic Church was the sole record-keeper of vital events (see Church records above). This survey could not retrieve a Louisiana-specific "Vital Records" wiki page (see Research tips); treat the sacramental registers as the vital-record substitute throughout 1699-1803.

### Immigration/military/tax/cemetery/newspaper records

| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Not applicable to this period (pre-1790) | not stated |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Not assessed for this period | not stated |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Not assessed for this period (no colonial-era Louisiana newspaper confirmed by this survey) | not stated |
| Fold3 | Military records | Not assessed for this period | not stated |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes total for Louisiana, 1699-1803 (both detailed above); this is the complete result set for that query, not a partial page. `catalog_search` for "Louisiana, United States" returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap for this survey, not evidence that no catalogued material exists; a narrower, single-parish search would likely do better.

### Physical repositories

| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories (partially digitized) | Physical visit; some materials digitized |

| Louisiana State Land Office | Spanish/French-era land grant records | Not stated by any tool result in this survey |

## Records NOT online
The Superior Council court/land/estate records at the Louisiana Historical Center are stated as only "partially digitized" — the remainder exists only in physical form there. The ANOM administrative correspondence and census rolls are described as held in France, with no online digitization confirmed by this survey. The New Orleans notarial archives (1730s onward) are described only as publicly accessible in person, with no online component confirmed.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that any specific Louisiana colonial record set was destroyed or lost. This guide does not claim any losses; absence of an online index for the Superior Council or notarial material reflects partial digitization, per the FamilySearch Wiki page cited, not loss.

## Research tips
- Search parish registers and the Superior Council's notarial/court records together — baptisms in Catholic registers and estate/contract records from the Superior Council are the two primary genealogical sources for this colony and period (FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).

The main sources are Catholic Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (the only legally recognized church then), starting around 1720 at the St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans, plus the colonial government's own records of land grants, contracts, court cases, and estate inventories, kept by a body called the Superior Council; both of these are only partly available online as unindexed photographed pages you have to browse by hand, written in French and Spanish, with the originals otherwise sitting in archives in New Orleans and, for some government correspondence and early censuses, in France itself. output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide produced for Pennsylvania coal mining towns in the late 1800s:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Guide (c. 1870–1900)

The guide focuses on Schuylkill County as the core anthracite region, with Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland Counties as closely related areas.

---

### Key Records for Coal Mining Families

#### Industry-Specific Sources
Pennsylvania's coal industry generated records not found elsewhere:
- **Mining company employment cards, payroll ledgers, and accident/fatality reports** — these are especially valuable because vital records were sparse. Some of these have been digitized for Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna Counties.
- Mine accident reports sometimes list a miner's age, nativity, and next of kin, making them a substitute for missing vital records.

#### Vital Records — Important Caveat
Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration during this period**. Statewide registration did not begin until 1906 (deaths) and 1915 (births). This means:
- **Birth records (pre-1906):** Look to church baptismal registers; no county birth registration existed.
- **Death records (pre-1906):** Church burial registers and cemetery records carry most of this burden.
- **Marriage records:** County courthouse marriage licenses and bonds, available locally at each county seat.

#### Church Records
Most coal-region immigrant families (Welsh, Irish, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Italian, Ukrainian) attended ethnic churches. Denominations vary by community:
- Catholic parishes (Irish, Polish, Slovak) — baptisms, marriages, burials
- Welsh Congregational and Welsh Baptist churches — often well-kept
- Greek Catholic and Orthodox churches for Eastern European immigrants

**Where to find them:** Some registers are held by the original parishes; others have been deposited with the Diocese of Allentown, the Diocese of Scranton, or deposited at county historical societies.

#### Federal Census Records (1870, 1880, 1900)
All three decennial censuses for this period are available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. They record:
- Household members, ages, birthplaces (and parents' birthplaces in 1880 and 1900)
- Occupation ("miner," "laborer in mines")
- State of nativity and country of origin

The 1890 census was largely destroyed, leaving a gap.

#### Pennsylvania State Census Substitutes
Pennsylvania had no state census in this era, so federal censuses and tax records fill the gaps.

#### Naturalization Records
Heavy immigrant populations make naturalization records important:
- Declarations of intent ("first papers") and petitions for naturalization were filed at the county Court of Common Pleas.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are held at the county courthouse; some have been filmed by FamilySearch.
- These records often give exact birthplace and arrival date — extremely valuable for tracing back to Europe.

#### Land and Tax Records
- County deed books and tax assessment lists can track a family's residence and economic status.
- Held at the county courthouse recorder of deeds.

---

### Primary Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville, PA) | Local histories, newspapers, some church and mining records |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society** (Scranton) | Records for the Wyoming Valley anthracite region |
| **Luzerne County Historical Society** (Wilkes-Barre) | Wyoming Valley records, Hazleton-area families |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | State-level records; some county originals transferred here |
| **FamilySearch** | Census, some naturalization films, some county records digitized |
| **County courthouses** (each county seat) | Marriage, naturalization, deed, and probate originals |

---

### Next Steps

Because mining families moved between coal-region counties for work, extending this survey to **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland Counties** individually is recommended. Each county has its own record holdings and historical society.

A direct inquiry to the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** or the county courthouse is likely needed to confirm specific holdings and access — no physical archive visit could be confirmed through online sources alone.

---

*Guide saved to the project research log as loc_001.*

- **Formed:** Schuylkill County formed 1811 (place_search: "Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States", dateRange +1811/). - **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.

args.guideSection:
### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906; before that, only Philadelphia County (from 1860) and Allegheny County (from 1870) registered locally — Schuylkill/Luzerne/Lackawanna/Carbon/Northumberland are not named among those early-registering counties (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- **What exists:** Statewide death certificates 1906-1968 are a FamilySearch collection, 4,218,763 people indexed (collection id 2255317). For births/deaths in the 1870-1900 target window, there is no statewide civil series.
- **Where held:** County-level marriage licenses/bonds from the colonial period, at the county courthouse; FamilySearch has microfilmed many of these (collection "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950", id 1921317, 1,048,378 people; "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950", id 1571957, 624,090 people; "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900", id 1502909, 397,530 people).
- **Gaps:** No state-level births/deaths for 1870-1900 in this window — this is a genuine gap, not a digitization gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms/burials) and the mine-worker/colliery records noted below under Other record types.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not individually confirmed by this survey.
- **Record types:** A FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) covers 1708-1985, 982,415 people indexed.
- **Where held:** Per collection above; parish/denominational archives for originals not confirmed by this survey.
- **Gaps:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Language:** Not confirmed by this survey; given the immigrant populations noted above, some registers may be in languages other than English — confirm per register.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Not separately surveyed here beyond the general note that federal decennial census runs from 1790; no Schuylkill-specific collection or volume was returned by the tools run in this survey.
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** None confirmed by this survey.
- **Access:** Not confirmed by this survey.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** A statewide FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" exists (id 1999196), but its personCount is 0 in this survey's result — likely unindexed/browse collection.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not applicable without a specific person.
- **Date range:** 1683-1994 per the collection above.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills, per general Pennsylvania practice; not separately confirmed for Schuylkill in this survey.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Plymouth Colony** (1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628/1629 charter) were separate jurisdictions until merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691**. Records before 1691 for Plymouth towns (Plymouth, Duxbury, Marshfield, etc.) were generated under Plymouth Colony's separate courts.
- The Great Migration (c. 1630–1640, ~20,000 settlers under Gov. John Winthrop) is the core immigration event for this period.
- **Dominant religion:** Congregational (Puritan), whose church records include membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings.

---

## Key Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Town-level birth/marriage/death registration was **mandated from 1639** — but nothing exists before that date from civil sources.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (id 2061550, ~3.4M people).
- The published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series covers 200+ towns and is often easier to use than the raw town books.
- **For events before 1639**, turn to church records instead.

### Church Records
- Congregational church records survive from the 1620s–1630s: membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (id 1921657, ~987K people).
- A digitized unindexed volume of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms (1630–1700, imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images) is **full-text searchable** on FamilySearch but is not name-indexed — use full-text search, not a name index.

### Probate Records
- Probate (wills, inventories, administrations) begins in the **1630s** at county probate courts.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (id 1678901, ~567K people).
- Originals also held at the **Massachusetts Archives** in Boston.

### Land & Town Proprietors' Records
- County-level deeds survive from the 1630s with "remarkably complete" runs.
- Early **town meeting and proprietors' records** (where land grants to settlers were recorded) exist as a digitized volume on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 1620–1698, 188 images) — but this is **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Military Records
- **Militia rolls from King Philip's War (1675–1676)** survive and are held at the Massachusetts Archives; some are published.

### Immigration Records
- No passenger-list collection for the Great Migration era (1630–1640) was found in these searches. Ship-passenger reconstructions for this period typically come from **published compiled sources** rather than a digitized record set.

### Court Records
- Colonial court records (General Court, county courts, Courts of General Sessions) document criminal, civil, and administrative actions. Held at the **Massachusetts Archives**, partially published.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (id 2061550) | Name-indexed |
| FamilySearch | Church Records, 1630–1920 (id 1921657) | Name-indexed |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | Name-indexed |
| FamilySearch (images) | Town Meeting/Proprietors' Records, 1620–1698 (img 007612044) | Browse-only; no index |
| FamilySearch (full-text) | Suffolk Co. Congregational Records, 1630–1700 (img 007612045) | Full-text searchable, not name-indexed |
| Find A Grave | findagrave.com | Cemetery/burial records |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Original colony records from 1620s, militia rolls, court records |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | Largest genealogical library in the region; compiled genealogies, manuscript collections |

---

## Critical Research Tips

1. **Plymouth Colony vs. Massachusetts Bay Colony:** Confirm which colony a town belonged to before searching — they kept entirely separate record systems until 1691.
2. **Pre-1639 events:** No civil vital registration existed before 1639; Congregational church records are your only substitute.
3. **Town vital records:** Use the published *"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"* series as your starting point — it's more usable than raw town books.
4. **Unindexed proprietors' volume (1620–1698):** Must be browsed image-by-image; no name search is possible.
5. **NEHGS** is the essential specialist repository for New England colonial genealogy and holds material not found through FamilySearch alone.

---

**Natural next step:** Identify the specific town(s) where your ancestor lived so a targeted research plan can be built around these record sets — especially since Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony records are searched separately.

## Locality Guide: Alabama, United States (c. 1798–1819, pre-statehood)

---

### Jurisdiction Overview

Alabama became a state in 1819. Before that, the region was part of the **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817)**, then the short-lived **Alabama Territory (1817–1819)**. Earlier still it was claimed by France, Britain, and Spain, with early European settlement concentrated around Mobile Bay (French, from 1702). Significant Anglo-American migration into the interior followed the **Creek War of 1813–1814**.

> ⚠️ **Important search tip:** FamilySearch's place system standardizes "Alabama" to the modern state starting from 1819, so searching under "Mississippi Territory," "Alabama Territory," or specific pre-1819 counties (like Washington County, Mississippi Territory) will likely surface more pre-statehood material than the modern state label will.

---

### Boundary Changes

The region passed through successive jurisdictions:
- **French** (1702–1763) → **British** (1763–1780) → **Spanish** (1780–1813, Mobile District) → **Mississippi Territory** (1798, expanded 1804) → **Alabama Territory** (1817) → **State of Alabama** (1819)

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide
**Coverage: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1860–1898**

### The Coal Region's Five Counties
The anthracite coal region spans **five counties**: Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. This guide focuses on **Schuylkill County** as the core county; the other four need their own separate surveys before you have the full picture.

---

### Key Record Types and What Survives

**Specialized Coal-Region Index — Start Here**

Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm which individual parishes' registers survive or are digitized beyond the one volume found; also collections_search surfaced a "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people).

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (pre-statehood, roughly 1760s–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Vermont was **not a stable jurisdiction** during this window. The territory was claimed by both the Province of New York and the Province of New Hampshire (as "the New Hampshire Grants"), operated as the self-declared, unrecognized **Vermont Republic from 1777**, and was finally admitted as the 14th U.S. state only in **1791** (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).

**Parent jurisdictions:** Claimed jointly by the Province of New York and Province of New Hampshire; self-governed de facto as the Vermont Republic, 1777–1791.

**Core historical context:** The defining event of this period is the land dispute — New Hampshire-issued township grants that New York refused to recognize — which shapes what records exist and where they were filed.

---

## Boundary Changes
Before 1791, the territory had no single stable civil jurisdiction. A family's pre-1791 records may be filed under:
- **New York colonial authority**, or
- **New Hampshire grant records**, or
- **Vermont Republic-era town/proprietors' records** (after 1777)

…depending on exactly when and where the event occurred.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857** — long after this period.
- Some **town clerk vital records survive unevenly back to the 1770s**; there is no comprehensive statewide pre-1791 series.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and town/proprietors' records (see below).

### Land Records ⭐ *Most Important for This Period*
- For this period, land grants were issued by the **Province of New Hampshire** ("New Hampshire Grants") and separately claimed/re-granted under **New York colonial authority**.
- The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — prepared under New York colonial authority — enumerates roughly **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize, with grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy").
- This schedule is described as the **earliest systematic resident list** for the future state.
- Exact current repository and online access were not confirmed by the tools used in this survey; this is a gap to investigate directly.

### Church Records
- Church registers often predate civil registration by decades, but no Vermont-specific denominational detail was returned by the tools used here — this is a known research gap. Investigating early congregational/church registers in a specific town should be a priority.

### Census Records
- The **first federal census (1790)** falls right at the edge of this period, taken while Vermont was transitioning into statehood.
- No pre-1791 provincial enumerations were confirmed in this survey.

### Probate and Court Records
- Not confirmed by any tool result for the pre-1791 period in this survey — a cataloguing/search gap, not proof such records don't exist.

### Military Records
- The **American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)** falls squarely within this period. Vermont forces/militia were active, but no specific Vermont Revolutionary War record sets or repositories were confirmed by the tools used here.

### Town Histories (Substitute Source) ✅
- 19th-century Vermont town histories, mostly published **1860–1900**, often **reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** otherwise hard to access — a named substitute source for pre-statehood material (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy").

---

## Online Repositories
Searches on FamilySearch for Vermont-specific digitized collections and volumes for 1760–1791 returned **no results in this survey** — a digitization/coverage gap, not necessarily proof nothing exists. It is worth checking FamilySearch directly.

General genealogy platforms (Ancestry, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) were returned as links but **without Vermont-specific pre-1791 collection counts or date ranges confirmed** in this session.

---

## Records NOT Yet Online (Known Gaps)
Based on this survey, the following were **not found in digitized online form**:
- The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (access/location unconfirmed)
- Surviving 1770s town clerk vital records
- Pre-1791 land/probate/court record series
- Pre-statehood church registers

This likely reflects a **digitization gap**, not evidence these records don't exist.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Treat pre-1791 Vermont as having no single civil jurisdiction of record.** Search under New York colonial land-grant records, New Hampshire grant records, *and* Vermont Republic-era town/proprietors' records together, since the New York–New Hampshire dispute is the defining fact of this period.

2. **Check the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** if an ancestor may have held a New Hampshire-issued township grant. It names grantee, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status — the best early roster of inhabitants.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced for **Yorkshire, England, 1851**:

---

## Yorkshire, England — Locality Guide for 1851 Death Records

### Civil Registration (the first place to look)
National civil registration of deaths began **1 July 1837**, so a death in 1851 *should* be recorded in the **General Register Office (GRO) death index**. How to access it:

- **FreeBMD** (free) — searchable index of GRO births, marriages, and deaths
- **GRO historical indexes online** (free) — the GRO's own digitized index; certificates ordered directly from the GRO
- **Ancestry** and **Findmypast** (subscription) — both hold the indexed GRO registers and in many cases the register images

Once you identify the index entry, you order the full death certificate from the GRO, which names the place, date, cause, informant, and sometimes the deceased's age and occupation.

> **Important caveat:** Enforcement of civil registration was still uneven in the late 1830s–early 1850s, so not every death was reported. If the civil record is missing, turn to church records next.

---

### Parish Burial Registers
If the civil death registration is absent or incomplete, **Anglican parish burial registers** are the main fallback. Yorkshire had hundreds of parishes. Original registers are typically held at:
- **West Yorkshire Archive Service** (Wakefield, Leeds, Bradford, Halifax, Huddersfield)
- **North Yorkshire County Record Office** (Northallerton)
- **Borthwick Institute for Archives**, University of York (ecclesiastical records, probate)

Many registers have been microfilmed and digitized. Search **Ancestry** (Yorkshire parish registers collection) and **Findmypast**.

---

### 1851 Census
The census was taken in **March 1851** — just months before or after a mid-1851 death. It can:
- Confirm where the person lived and with whom
- Identify the age, birthplace, and occupation (useful for distinguishing same-name individuals)

The 1851 census for Yorkshire is fully indexed and freely searchable on **FamilySearch** and by subscription on Ancestry and Findmypast.

---

### Important Search Note — Yorkshire's Sub-divisions
Yorkshire was historically divided into three **Ridings**:
- **West Riding** (Leeds, Sheffield, Bradford, Wakefield, Halifax)
- **North Riding** (York, Scarborough, Whitby, Richmond)
- **East Riding** (Hull, Beverley, Bridlington)

Online records are very often catalogued under the specific Riding — or under "West Yorkshire," "North Yorkshire," or "East Yorkshire" — rather than under "Yorkshire" as a whole. **Run searches both ways** (the full county name and the specific Riding) to avoid missing records.

---

### Where to Search

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FreeBMD** | GRO death index 1837–1983 | Free |
| **GRO (gov.uk)** | Full death certificates | Paid certificate order |
| **FamilySearch** | 1851 census; many parish registers | Free |
| **Ancestry** | GRO registers; parish registers; census | Subscription |
| **Findmypast** | Strong Yorkshire coverage; GRO; parish | Subscription |
| **West Yorkshire Archive Service** | Original parish/nonconformist registers | In-person or online catalogue |
| **Borthwick Institute, York** | Ecclesiastical records, probate | In-person or catalogue |

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Search the **GRO death index** (via FreeBMD or Findmypast) for the person's name, estimated quarter of 1851, and registration district.
2. If found, order the **full death certificate** from the GRO.
3. If not found in civil registration, search **parish burial registers** on Ancestry or Findmypast under the relevant Riding.
4. Cross-reference with the **1851 census** to confirm the person's location and household before death.

A research plan can be built from this guide to systematically work through these sources for your specific ancestor. Just share the name and any known details.

dimensions.rationale: The guide provides a search order: start with the GRO death index (FreeBMD free, or subscription sites), then check parish burial registers if not found, use the 1851 census to confirm household/location, and search under both Yorkshire and Riding names. It cites specific FamilySearch collection IDs (2285341, 2563939, 4439317, 4319956) and external repositories (FreeBMD, Findmypast, Ancestry). It identifies pitfalls: incomplete early registration enforcement, records filed under Riding names rather than 'Yorkshire', and the need to search multiple quarters of the GRO index. However, it omits Yorkshire BMD (http://www.yorkshirebmd.org.uk/) as a specific regional index to search, which the external_links_search returned and the per-test context requires naming. This is a concrete gap in the strategy for a Yorkshire-specific resource.
